answer.origin: BofA Research characterization of AMD's own modeled estimates, reported by Investing.com and syndicated on Yahoo Finance; the original AMD estimate date and publication are not stated in the record.
answer.note: Third-party relay of AMD's vendor-modeled claim: in a modeled 100kW rack deployment, AMD estimates EPYC 9965 (Turin) delivers about 2.4x the rack-level throughput of an NVIDIA Vera baseline, and projects EPYC 6 (Venice) at about 3.3x. Conditional read for NVDA: this is a competitive-positioning claim that pressures how Vera's value is framed (per-rack throughput versus latency and GPU utilization), not evidence of NVDA revenue, orders or Vera share. Because it is a vendor model, its weight is limited to showing the metric AMD intends to contest on; it does not establish measured performance or buyer adoption.
limitations: The modeled workload, software stack, Vera baseline configuration and throughput definition are not disclosed in the record, so the 2.4x and 3.3x figures cannot be tied to a specific comparison.
The 2.4x and 3.3x values are AMD estimates as characterized by BofA; no independent benchmark or AMD primary document is in the record.
The date of AMD's estimate and whether it was made for AI 2026 Day are not stated.
Venice figure is a forward projection of an unreleased product and carries no shipment or availability timing in the record.
No NVDA Vera revenue, shipment or customer data is in the record, so this claim does not measure NVDA's CPU demand.
follow_up: Locate AMD's primary AI 2026 Day materials or product documentation for the 100kW rack model and check the stated Vera baseline, workload and throughput definition.
Look for independent or third-party benchmarks comparing Vera with EPYC 9965 on agentic or rack-level throughput workloads.
Check NVDA disclosures or Vera launch materials for any response to the per-rack throughput framing and for Vera availability dates.
